title: A Doll's House
author: Henrik Ibsen
setting: One room in the Helmers' flat in a Norwegian town, across Christmas Eve, Christmas Day and the evening after
lengthNote: Three acts in prose, all in the same room, with every decisive event of the past reported rather than shown
openingLine: Hide the Christmas tree carefully, Helen. Be sure the children do not see it until this evening, when it is dressed.
summary: Nora Helmer forged her dying father's signature to borrow money that saved her husband's life, and has been paying it back in secret for years out of the housekeeping. Over three days at Christmas the loan comes due socially rather than financially: the man who holds the bond wants a job, the letter reaches the letterbox, and Nora waits for her husband to do the thing she has always assumed he would do. He does not, and the play ends with the most consequential exit in modern theatre.
referenceStyle: act. The translation checked against runs as continuous prose dialogue without line numbers, so quotations are placed by act and by the moment in the action rather than by line.

sourceText.label: Standard Ebooks text of A Doll's House, in R. Farquharson Sharp's English translation
sourceText.note: Ibsen wrote in Danish-Norwegian; every English quotation here is a translator's wording. Sharp anglicises some of the money, so the Porter is paid in shillings where Ibsen's has krone. The text carries no line numbering, so references give the act.

atAGlance.label: Published
atAGlance.note: As Et dukkehjem, in Copenhagen, in a first printing of 8,000 copies.

atAGlance.label: First performed
atAGlance.note: At the Royal Theatre, Copenhagen, with Betty Hennings as Nora.

atAGlance.label: English text here
atAGlance.note: His translation was published by J. M. Dent in Everyman's Library in 1910.

atAGlance.label: Shape
atAGlance.note: The forgery, the illness, the father's death and the journey to Italy all happen before the curtain rises.

structure.label: Act I
structure.title: Christmas Eve: a tree, a promotion and a bond
structure.summary: Nora comes home with parcels and is teased about spending. Mrs Linde arrives looking for work, and Nora tells her the secret she has kept for eight years. Krogstad, who lent the money and holds a bond with a forged signature on it, comes to ask for his job at the bank and makes plain what he will do if he loses it.

scenes.summary: The skylark and the squirrel, the macaroons hidden in a pocket, and a household about to have money for the first time.
Nora tells Mrs Linde that the journey to Italy was paid for by her, not by her father.
The lender explains what the forged signature is worth to him.
Helmer lectures on how a deceitful parent poisons a household, and Nora sends the children away.

structure.label: Act II
structure.title: Christmas Day: the tree stripped, the letterbox locked
structure.summary: The tree stands bare in the corner and the letter has not yet come. Nora tries to get Krogstad's dismissal reversed and fails on a point of Helmer's pride; Doctor Rank makes his declaration at the worst possible moment; and the letter goes into the box, which Helmer keeps the key to. Nora dances the tarantella to stop him opening it.

scenes.summary: The fancy-dress dress needs mending, and Mrs Linde begins asking questions about Doctor Rank.
Helmer refuses to keep Krogstad on, and the reason turns out to be that the man calls him by his Christian name.
The black cross, and a request Nora can no longer make once he has spoken.
Krogstad drops his letter in the box; Nora dances to hold her husband's attention for twenty-four hours.

structure.label: Act III
structure.title: After the ball: two shipwrecked people, and one door
structure.summary: Mrs Linde and Krogstad settle their own past in ten minutes and she stops him withdrawing the letter, on the grounds that the Helmers need the truth more than they need safety. Helmer reads it, calls his wife a hypocrite and a criminal, reads the second letter, declares himself saved, and finds that the crisis has gone the wrong way round.

scenes.summary: Two people who lost each other for money agree to join forces.
Helmer's fear for his own position, and his plan to keep up appearances.
The bond is returned, Helmer forgives, and Nora changes her dress.
The first serious conversation of the marriage, conducted sitting down, and the door below.

characters.name: Nora Helmer
characters.summary: She has run a secret business for eight years, copying documents at night behind a locked door and calling it fun, while playing the spendthrift child her husband finds charming. The play's argument is that the performance and the competence are the same woman, and that nobody in the house has ever been curious enough to notice.
characters.clue: She eats macaroons in secret, saved her husband's life with a forged signature, and dances a tarantella to stop a letter being read.

relationships.label: brought up by, and employer of

characters.name: Torvald Helmer
characters.role: A lawyer, newly appointed manager of the bank
characters.summary: He is not a villain and is barely even unkind; he is a man who has arranged his household as a compliment to himself and cannot imagine it any other way. His refusal to keep Krogstad on turns out to rest on the fact that the man uses his first name, and that detail is the whole diagnosis.
characters.clue: He calls his wife a lark and a squirrel, lectures her on the household effects of a deceitful mother, and cannot dismiss an employee for the reason he gives.

characters.name: Nils Krogstad
characters.role: A subordinate at the bank, and Nora's creditor
characters.summary: He committed one forgery, was never prosecuted and has been paying for it socially ever since, which makes him the play's best witness on how respectability actually works. He is threatening for two acts and then, given one thing he wants, becomes reasonable in a page.
characters.clue: He did once what Nora has done, and has spent years finding out what it costs afterwards.

characters.name: Mrs Linde
characters.role: Nora's old schoolfriend, a widow looking for work
characters.summary: She married for money to keep a mother and two brothers alive, was widowed with nothing, and is the only character in the play who has supported herself. Her decision to let the letter stand is the hinge of the last act, and she takes it for a reason she states plainly: this house has been living on concealment.
characters.clue: She gave up the man she loved to support her family, and now asks a favour that turns out to cost her friend everything.
traits: decisive at the wrong moment for Nora

characters.name: Doctor Rank
characters.role: The family's friend and daily visitor
characters.summary: He is dying of a disease he attributes to his father's manner of living, and he keeps the fact from Helmer because Helmer cannot bear ugliness. His declaration to Nora removes the one source of money she had left, and his exit is arranged by visiting card so that nobody has to watch.
characters.clue: He will send a card with a black cross on it when the end begins, and asks to be allowed to die out of sight.
traits: in love with his friend's wife

characters.name: Anne
characters.summary: She gave up her own child to take a position, which is the same transaction Nora is about to make and the play puts them side by side without comment. She has two short scenes and they carry the entire cost of the ending in advance.
characters.clue: She nursed the mistress of the house when she was small, and left her own daughter behind to do it.

relationships.label: nurse to, then to her children

themes.name: The doll, and the performance of a marriage
themes.summary: Nora is addressed as a bird, a squirrel and a child for two and a half acts, and answers in the same register because it works. When she finally describes the arrangement, she does it as a line of descent: her father played with her, Torvald played with her, and she has been playing with her own children in exactly the same way.
themes.development: Pet names and a hidden bag of macaroons in Act I; a costume, a rehearsed dance and a husband as audience in Act II; and in Act III the word doll used by Nora herself, at a table, with the tarantella dress changed for ordinary clothes.

themes.name: Money, law and a woman's signature
themes.summary: The plot depends on a legal fact rather than a moral one: Nora could not borrow without a man's name, so she wrote her dying father's. Krogstad's answer, that the law cares nothing about motives, is not cruelty but an accurate statement of the position, and the play lets it stand unrefuted.
themes.development: A secret debt repaid out of housekeeping in Act I, a bond in a letterbox in Act II, and in Act III a woman announcing that she will find out whether the law or she is right.

themes.name: Reputation and what a man will risk
themes.summary: Helmer's whole conduct is governed by how things look to the bank. He will not keep Krogstad because the man addresses him familiarly in front of the staff, and when the letter arrives his first thought is not for his wife but for whether he might be suspected of prompting her.
themes.development: A promotion in Act I, a refusal on a point of manners in Act II, and in Act III a proposal that the marriage continue in the eyes of the world while ceasing in every other respect.

themes.name: Duties to others and duties to oneself
themes.summary: The last fifteen minutes are an argument about the word duty, conducted at a table with both parties sitting down. Helmer names the duties of a wife and mother as though listing established facts; Nora accepts them as widely held opinions and says she must first find out whether they are true for her.
themes.development: Sacred duties asserted, other duties just as sacred claimed, and then the shortest and most disruptive line in the play: duties to myself.

themes.name: Inheritance, sickness and the sins of fathers
themes.summary: Helmer believes moral corruption passes from parent to child and says so at length in Act I, not knowing whose household he is describing. Rank's spinal disease is attributed to his father's amusements, so the play sets a medical inheritance beside a moral one and declines to separate them cleanly.
themes.development: A lawyer's theory of deceitful mothers in Act I, a dying man's account of his father in Act II, and a mother in Act III who concludes that she is unfit to bring up children until she has educated herself.

themes.name: Work, and who is allowed to do it
themes.summary: Every character is defined by employment: a new managership, a subordinate clerkship, a widow looking for a post, a nurse who left her own child to take one, and a wife whose earnings had to be hidden because she was not supposed to have any. Nora describes the copying she did at night as the happiest work she has known.
themes.development: Secret night work in Act I, a job asked for and refused in Act II, and in Act III a woman leaving with nothing and intending to find something to do.

techniques.name: Analytic structure
techniques.definition: A play whose decisive events all happened before the curtain rose and reach the audience as disclosure.
techniques.inThisBook: The forgery, the illness, the journey to Italy and the father's death are all in the past; the three acts are the process by which they come out, which is why so much of the play is people telling each other things.

techniques.name: The single room
techniques.definition: Confining every scene to one interior so that entrances and exits carry the pressure.
techniques.inThisBook: Nothing can be escaped except by leaving, which is why the final door has the force it does; the same doors admit Krogstad, Rank and the letter.

techniques.name: Stage properties
techniques.definition: Objects that carry meaning and change state across the acts.
techniques.inThisBook: The Christmas tree is dressed in Act I and stripped in Act II; the macaroons, the locked letterbox, the fancy-dress costume and the returned bond each mark a stage of the concealment.

techniques.name: Diminutive address
techniques.definition: Characterising a relationship through the names one person is allowed to use for another.
techniques.inThisBook: Lark, squirrel, skylark, spendthrift, little person: Helmer almost never uses his wife's name in the first two acts, and the moment he starts to she has stopped answering.

techniques.name: The set-piece dance
techniques.definition: A performance inside the play that the audience watches being performed.
techniques.inThisBook: Nora rehearses the tarantella wildly to keep her husband from the letterbox; he corrects her steps, which tells us exactly what he thinks he is watching.

techniques.name: The parallel couple
techniques.definition: A second pairing whose arrangement comments on the first.
techniques.inThisBook: Mrs Linde and Krogstad negotiate their future in one honest conversation, which is the thing the Helmers have never once managed, and they do it in the same room.

quotations.text: Is that my little lark twittering out there?
quotations.speaker: Helmer
quotations.context: His first words in the play, called from the study without coming out.
quotations.analysis: The first thing said to Nora is not her name, and it is a question about a noise rather than a person. Ibsen puts the whole marriage in the opening exchange: a man who addresses his wife as wildlife, from another room, and a woman who answers in the character he has named.

quotations.text: It was I who saved Torvald’s life.
quotations.speaker: Nora
quotations.context: Pulling Mrs Linde down beside her on the sofa, after being told she knows nothing of real trouble.
quotations.analysis: The emphasis is placed on the pronoun, and it is the first sentence in the play in which Nora is the subject of a serious verb. She has been treated as an expense for two scenes and now produces the one fact that would reverse the household's opinion of her, and immediately makes her friend promise to keep it.

quotations.text: The law cares nothing about motives.
quotations.speaker: Krogstad
quotations.context: Answering Nora's claim that saving a life must count for something.
quotations.analysis: Six words, and they are the play's legal position stated correctly by its least admired character. Ibsen gives the blackmailer the accurate account of how the statute works, so that Nora's outrage has nothing to push against except the law itself.

quotations.text: Then it must be a very foolish law.
quotations.speaker: Nora
quotations.context: Her immediate reply to Krogstad.
quotations.analysis: She dismisses the entire legal code in eight words and then changes the subject, which in Act I reads as childishness. The last act picks the same sentence up and turns it into a programme: she will go away and find out whether the law is right or she is.

quotations.text: Almost everyone who has gone to the bad early in life has had a deceitful mother.
quotations.speaker: Helmer
quotations.context: Explaining to Nora, minutes after Krogstad has left the house, why a dishonest parent ruins children.
quotations.analysis: He delivers it as professional experience and it lands on the woman standing in front of him, who has just been threatened over a forged signature. The scene ends with Nora refusing to let the children in, which is the first thing she decides entirely on her own.

quotations.text: He suffers from a diseased moral character, Mrs. Helmer; but even he began talking of its being highly important that he should live.
quotations.speaker: Doctor Rank
quotations.context: Explaining who else is waiting to see Helmer.
quotations.analysis: A dying physician diagnoses a man's ethics as a medical condition, and the sentence turns on the word but: even the morally diseased want to go on living. Ibsen is putting Rank's spine and Krogstad's reputation into the same vocabulary, which is the play's quiet joke about inheritance.

quotations.text: Do you suppose I am going to make myself ridiculous before my whole staff, to let people think that I am a man to be swayed by all sorts of outside influence?
quotations.speaker: Helmer
quotations.context: Refusing to reinstate Krogstad at his wife's request.
quotations.analysis: The reason he gives is not that Krogstad is dishonest but that reversing himself would look like being led by someone. A few lines later he admits the real objection is that the man calls him by his first name in front of the clerks, and a marriage is destroyed on that point of etiquette.

quotations.text: As soon as I am quite certain that the worst has come, I shall send you my card with a black cross on it, and then you will know that the loathsome end has begun.
quotations.speaker: Doctor Rank
quotations.context: Telling Nora how she will know that he is dying.
quotations.analysis: He arranges his own death as a piece of correspondence, so that nobody has to be present for it. The card with the black cross is the play's most economical stage property: it converts a man into a piece of paper in a letterbox, which is precisely what Krogstad's letter does to Nora.

quotations.text: How should you understand it? A wonderful thing is going to happen!
quotations.speaker: Nora
quotations.context: To Mrs Linde, who has asked what she is waiting for.
quotations.analysis: She never says what the wonderful thing is, and the refusal is not coyness: naming it would require her to admit she has been counting on her husband to sacrifice himself. The phrase recurs half a dozen times and means something different each time she uses it.

quotations.text: You should have let it alone; you must prevent nothing. After all, it is splendid to be waiting for a wonderful thing to happen.
quotations.speaker: Nora
quotations.context: On being told that Mrs Linde has written to Krogstad and will see him tomorrow.
quotations.analysis: She forbids the one intervention that might save her, because the catastrophe has become the test she wants her husband to pass. It is the clearest evidence that by Act II Nora is no longer trying to avoid discovery; she is waiting for it.

quotations.text: Two on the same piece of wreckage would stand a better chance than each on their own.
quotations.speaker: Mrs Linde
quotations.context: Proposing to Krogstad in the Helmers' sitting room while the dance goes on upstairs.
quotations.analysis: A proposal expressed as arithmetic, offered by a woman who has already once chosen security over love and does not pretend otherwise. This is the only negotiation in the play conducted by two people who tell each other the truth, and Ibsen stages it in the same room that has held eight years of concealment.

quotations.text: Helmer must know all about it. This unhappy secret must be disclosed; they must have a complete understanding between them, which is impossible with all this concealment and falsehood going on.
quotations.speaker: Mrs Linde
quotations.context: Stopping Krogstad from asking for his letter back.
quotations.analysis: She takes the decision that ends the marriage, and she takes it on a principle rather than out of malice: a household running on a secret is worse off than one facing a scandal. Everything Nora suffers in the last twenty minutes is set in motion by the only person in the play who has been supporting herself.

quotations.text: Now you have destroyed all my happiness. You have ruined all my future. It is horrible to think of! I am in the power of an unscrupulous man; he can do what he likes with me, ask anything he likes of me, give me any orders he pleases⁠—I dare not refuse. And I must sink to such miserable depths because of a thoughtless woman!
quotations.speaker: Helmer
quotations.context: Moments after reading Krogstad's letter.
quotations.analysis: Count the possessives: my happiness, my future, my house. The forgery was committed to keep him alive and his response is a list of his own losses, which is the exact information Nora has been waiting eight years to receive.

quotations.text: Yes, it is true! I am saved! Nora, I am saved!
quotations.speaker: Helmer
quotations.context: Opening the second letter, which encloses the bond.
quotations.analysis: He says it twice and both times in the first person singular, then adds her name as an afterthought rather than as a subject. Nora's question in reply, what about her, gets the answer that she is saved too, and the pronouns have already decided the end of the play.

quotations.text: He called me his doll-child, and he played with me just as I used to play with my dolls.
quotations.speaker: Nora
quotations.context: At the table, explaining how she came to have no opinions of her own.
quotations.analysis: The word the play is named for is used by Nora only in the last ten minutes, and she applies it first to her father. What she is describing is not cruelty but an inheritance of arrangements, which is why the speech is delivered flatly rather than as an accusation.

quotations.text: But our home has been nothing but a playroom. I have been your doll-wife, just as at home I was Papa’s doll-child; and here the children have been my dolls. I thought it great fun when you played with me, just as they thought it great fun when I played with them. That is what our marriage has been, Torvald.
quotations.speaker: Nora
quotations.context: Continuing the same speech, a few lines later.
quotations.analysis: Three generations are lined up in one sentence: she was played with, she was played with again, and she has been doing it to her own children. The charge is not that her husband was a tyrant but that nothing in the house was ever serious, and she includes herself in the indictment.

quotations.text: Before all else, you are a wife and a mother.
quotations.speaker: Helmer
quotations.context: Answering Nora's claim that she has duties to herself.
quotations.analysis: He states it as a definition rather than an argument, which is what makes it answerable. The phrase before all else is then taken from him word for word in Nora's reply, and the theft of the construction is the point at which she stops being managed.

quotations.text: Duties to myself.
quotations.speaker: Nora
quotations.context: Asked what duties could possibly outrank those to husband and children.
quotations.analysis: Three words, and they are the sentence that caused the play to be banned, rewritten and argued about across Europe. Ibsen places them as a flat answer to a rhetorical question, with no justification attached, so that the audience has to supply the argument or refuse it.

quotations.text: I don’t believe that any longer. I believe that before all else I am a reasonable human being, just as you are⁠—or, at all events, that I must try and become one. I know quite well, Torvald, that most people would think you right, and that views of that kind are to be found in books; but I can no longer content myself with what most people say, or with what is found in books. I must think over things for myself and get to understand them.
quotations.speaker: Nora
quotations.context: Rejecting the definition of herself as wife and mother first.
quotations.analysis: She does not claim that most people are wrong, only that she can no longer take their word or a book's for it. The demand is not for rights but for the chance to find out what she thinks, which is a smaller and much harder thing to refuse.

quotations.text: According to it a woman has no right to spare her old dying father, or to save her husband’s life. I can’t believe that.
quotations.speaker: Nora
quotations.context: Explaining what she has learned about the law since Krogstad explained it to her.
quotations.analysis: She has taken Krogstad's legal lesson from Act I and turned it into a test the law has to pass, not one she has to. The last four words do all the work: not a claim about what the law is, but a refusal to accept it, which is where the play leaves the question.

quotations.text: I would gladly work night and day for you, Nora⁠—bear sorrow and want for your sake. But no man would sacrifice his honour for the one he loves.
quotations.speaker: Helmer
quotations.context: Told that the wonderful thing she waited for was his taking the blame himself.
quotations.analysis: The first clause offers a lifetime of labour and the second withholds the one thing that was actually asked for, and he sees no contradiction between them. Honour is being described as a possession a man cannot spend, which is the same logic his household has applied to money all along.

quotations.text: It is a thing hundreds of thousands of women have done.
quotations.speaker: Nora
quotations.context: Her reply, immediately after Helmer says no man would sacrifice his honour for love.
quotations.analysis: The sentence answers a claim about human nature with a fact about how many people have already done it. It also enlarges the play in one line, taking a quarrel in a Norwegian sitting room and setting it against every household the audience has come from.

quotations.text: Ah, Torvald, the most wonderful thing of all would have to happen.
quotations.speaker: Nora
quotations.context: Asked whether they might ever be more than strangers.
quotations.analysis: The phrase has been running through the play attached to a rescue she expected from her husband, and here it is transferred to something neither of them can arrange: a change in both of them. She says two lines later that she no longer believes in wonderful things happening, which is what makes the ending a departure rather than an ultimatum.

quotations.text: The sound of a door shutting is heard from below.
quotations.speaker: Stage direction
quotations.context: The last line of the play, printed as a stage direction after Helmer's final half-sentence.
quotations.analysis: Ibsen gives the curtain to a noise offstage rather than to a speech, and to a door that the audience never sees. The sentence is passive and impersonal, which leaves Helmer alone on stage with a hope he has just voiced and a sound that answers it.

timeline.label: Henrik Ibsen born at Skien
timeline.detail: His father's business failed when he was a boy, and money and social standing recur throughout his work.

timeline.label: Peer Gynt published
timeline.detail: The last of the great verse plays before Ibsen turned to contemporary prose drama.

timeline.label: Pillars of Society published
timeline.detail: The first of the modern prose plays, and the beginning of the sequence this play belongs to.

timeline.label: Et dukkehjem published in Copenhagen
timeline.detail: Published on 4 December in a first printing of 8,000 copies.

timeline.label: First performance at the Royal Theatre, Copenhagen
timeline.detail: On 21 December, with Betty Hennings as Nora.

timeline.label: Ibsen supplies an alternative ending for the German stage
timeline.detail: In it Nora does not leave; his letter of February 1880 explains that he wrote it himself only to stop somebody else doing it worse.

timeline.label: Ibsen's Ghosts published
timeline.detail: Often read as his reply to those who had wanted Nora to stay: a marriage nobody leaves, and what it costs.

timeline.label: First public British production
timeline.detail: At the Novelty Theatre, London, on 7 June, with Janet Achurch as Nora and Charles Charrington as Helmer, in William Archer's translation.

timeline.label: Ibsen returns to Norway
timeline.detail: After twenty-seven years living in Italy and Germany.

timeline.label: Ibsen dies in Kristiania
timeline.detail: By then his contemporary plays were established across Europe and had reshaped what a serious stage play could be about.

timeline.label: R. Farquharson Sharp's translation published
timeline.detail: Issued by J. M. Dent in Everyman's Library; it is the English text these quotations are checked against.

places.name: Skien, Norway
places.note: Ibsen's birthplace, and the town whose commercial collapse shaped his sense of respectability and debt.

places.name: Rome
places.note: Where Ibsen was living when he began the play; he spent twenty-seven years out of Norway.

places.name: Amalfi
places.note: Where he worked on the play through the summer of 1879, on the coast south of Naples.

places.name: Copenhagen
places.note: The Royal Theatre, where the play was first performed on 21 December 1879.

places.name: Kristiania (Oslo)
places.note: The Norwegian capital, and the city Ibsen returned to in 1891 and died in.

places.name: London
places.note: The Novelty Theatre, where the first public British production opened in June 1889 and started the English argument about Nora.

criticalViews.position: A play about the position of women
criticalViews.summary: The reading the play has carried since 1879, and the reason it was banned, rewritten and imitated: a wife discovers that the law, her marriage and her upbringing have all treated her as a minor, and leaves to find out what she thinks.
criticalViews.counter: Ibsen himself resisted being enrolled as a campaigner, and the play is at least as interested in Helmer's fear of his colleagues as in Nora's rights.

criticalViews.position: A play about being a self at all
criticalViews.summary: A broader reading takes the subject to be the duty of any person to become something other than what their household has made them, with Nora's sex as the circumstance that makes the demand visible rather than its cause.
criticalViews.counter: It risks making the legal details of the forgery decorative, when the plot depends entirely on what a married woman could and could not sign.

criticalViews.summary: Criticism of the staging has emphasised what Ibsen did to the well-made play: an ordinary room, contemporary clothes, a plot made of paper and post, and a final act in which two people sit down and talk instead of embracing or dying.
criticalViews.counter: The machinery is still that of melodrama, with a blackmailer, a bond, a lost letter and a coincidence of old lovers, however soberly it is handled.

essayQuestions.question: How does Ibsen present the Helmers' marriage before the crisis breaks?
essayQuestions.focus: Language, pet names and performance in Acts I and II
plan: Open on the first exchange: a husband addressing a bird from another room and a wife answering in character.
Collect the vocabulary of ownership and smallness, and note how rarely Helmer uses his wife's name.
Set against it what Nora has actually been doing: night work, secret repayments and eight years of accounts.
Use the tarantella as the moment the performance becomes literal, with Helmer correcting the steps.
Conclude on Act III, where Nora describes the arrangement in her own words and the vocabulary stops working.

essayQuestions.question: 'Krogstad is right about the law and Nora is right about everything else.' Discuss.
plan: Set out the legal facts: what Nora signed, why she could not sign her own name, and what the bond is worth.
Read Krogstad's statement about motives as an accurate account rather than a threat.
Trace Nora's answer from her dismissal of a foolish law in Act I to her decision in Act III to test it.
Consider Krogstad's own history as evidence of what the law does after it has finished with someone.
Weigh what the play settles and what it deliberately leaves to the audience.

essayQuestions.question: What is the function of Mrs Linde and Doctor Rank?
essayQuestions.focus: The parallel plot and the play's other lives
plan: Establish Mrs Linde's history: a marriage for money, a widowhood with nothing, and work as survival.
Examine her decision to let Krogstad's letter stand, and the principle she gives for it.
Set the Linde and Krogstad conversation beside any conversation the Helmers have before Act III.
Read Rank as the play's other inheritance, and his removal of Nora's last financial option.
Assess whether the subplots comment on the marriage, cause its collapse, or both.

essayQuestions.question: Is the ending of A Doll's House earned?
essayQuestions.focus: The last act, the argument about duty, and the door
plan: Describe what changes in the staging of the final act: ordinary clothes, a table, two chairs and a conversation.
Track the argument through the words sacred, duty and religion, and note who keeps redefining them.
Weigh the objection that Nora changes too fast against the evidence of her competence in Acts I and II.
Consider the children, whom she leaves, and her own reason for doing so.
Close on Ibsen's alternative German ending and what its existence shows about how the original was received.

discussionQuestions: Nora has run a secret loan for eight years without anyone noticing. Does the play's ending come out of nowhere, or has it been in front of us all along?
Helmer will not keep Krogstad because the man uses his first name in front of the staff. Is that a small thing or the whole diagnosis?
Mrs Linde stops Krogstad withdrawing the letter. Is she right to?
Nora leaves her children with the nurse who once left her own child to look after Nora. What is Ibsen doing by putting those two facts in the same play?
